modules.title: DevOps at Cloud-Native Parity
modules.summary: Welcome to IL-05 — Cloud DevSecOps Platform SRE. I'm your instructor for this course, and we start where every platform career starts: the DevOps toolchain, in adoption order. This is Module 1: DevOps at Cloud-Native Parity. We'll map the seven DevOps roles and their boundaries, build Linux/shell/Git fluency with real branching and PR discipline, containerize with Docker (images, layers, multi-stage builds), ship through Jenkins pipelines as code with security gates, deploy to Kubernetes, hold fleet state with Ansible, and observe it all with Prometheus, Grafana, and Loki. Every tool earns its place against a running system — the milestone arc is containerize, then pipeline, then deploy, then observe.
objectives: Map the seven DevOps roles and their boundaries; sequence your own path.
Build Docker images with multi-stage builds; explain layers and caching.
Write Jenkins pipelines as code with artifact management and security gates.
Deploy to Kubernetes: pods, services, deployments, ConfigMaps/secrets, ingress, Helm.
Query Prometheus with PromQL; build Grafana dashboards and alerts.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
The vocabulary of the toolchain — every term here appears in the objectives, the procedure, and the quiz.
- **DevOps roles** — build, release, operate, observe, secure, automate, collaborate; the seven roles whose boundaries vary by org and give this path its sequence.
- **trunk-based branching** — short-lived branches merged straight to main; fits small teams and fast cadences.
- **GitFlow** — a branching model with release trains and more ceremony; fits scheduled releases, at the cost of overhead.
- **monorepo** — one repository for many services; buys atomic cross-service changes, costs tooling complexity.
- **polyrepo** — one repository per service; buys team autonomy, costs versioning and coordination overhead.
- **DORA metrics** — the industry-standard delivery performance signals; review latency is one of them in disguise.
- **Docker image** — a packaged, immutable filesystem-plus-metadata unit built from a Dockerfile.
- **Docker layer** — each Dockerfile instruction creates a cached layer; ordering instructions for cache hits is a core skill.
- **multi-stage build** — compile in a fat build stage, copy only the artifact into a slim runtime stage; an 800MB build environment becomes a ~15MB image.
- **registry** — where images live; tagging discipline means immutable tags for releases.
- **pipeline as code** — the Jenkins pipeline defined in a Jenkinsfile, versioned with the repo.
- **security scanning gate** — SAST and dependency scans placed in the pipeline before push/deploy; the build fails, not the audit.
- **SBOM** — software bill of materials; the inventory of what's inside an artifact.
- **Kubernetes pod** — the smallest deployable unit: one or more containers sharing network and storage.
- **deployment** — the workload controller that runs rolling updates of pods.
- **ConfigMap** — non-sensitive configuration injected as env vars or files.
- **Kubernetes secret** — base64-encoded (not encrypted) configuration; the real security boundary is etcd encryption plus RBAC.
- **ingress** — the cluster's HTTP(S) front door, routing external traffic to services.
- **Helm chart** — a package of Kubernetes manifests; charts are the packaging format.
- **Ansible playbook** — the idempotent fleet-state definition; roles organize reusable playbooks.
- **ansible-vault** — encrypts secret variables at rest in version control; distinct from HashiCorp Vault.
- **PromQL** — the Prometheus query language; `rate(http_requests_total[5m])` is the per-second request rate over a 5-minute window.
- **RED method** — Rate, Errors, Duration: the request-centric dashboard method.
- **USE method** — Utilization, Saturation, Errors: the resource-centric dashboard method.
- **readiness probe** — gates traffic to a pod; zero-downtime rolling updates are a probe configuration.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Prove each tool against a running system, in adoption order. You will containerize a small web app, gate it through a pipeline, deploy it to Kubernetes, and observe it — the milestone arc from this module.
1. **Containerize.** Write a multi-stage Dockerfile: `FROM golang:1.22 AS build` compiles the app, then `FROM gcr.io/distroless/static` ships only the binary. Put slow-changing instructions (dependency install) early and `COPY . .` last, so source edits don't bust the dependency cache.
2. **Pipeline.** Write a Jenkinsfile with stages lint, test, build, scan, push, deploy — with a gate between each. Place the SAST/dependency scan before push so a vulnerable artifact never reaches the registry; store the SBOM with the artifact.
3. **Deploy.** Apply a Deployment with a readiness probe, expose it with a Service and Ingress, and externalize config into a ConfigMap (secrets into a Secret, knowing they're base64). Roll the Deployment and watch the readiness probe hold traffic off new pods until they answer.
4. **Observe.** Point Prometheus at the app, query `rate(http_requests_total[5m])` in PromQL, build a Grafana dashboard on the RED method, and add one alert: page on user-facing symptoms (latency, error rate), ticket on causes (disk filling).
5. **Fleet state.** Write an Ansible playbook that converges a VM to the same baseline idempotently; store its secrets with ansible-vault.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Ship the milestone arc end to end: a containerized service, built by a Jenkins pipeline with a security gate, deployed to Kubernetes with zero-downtime rolling updates, observed in Grafana with a RED dashboard and one paging alert. Deliverables: the multi-stage Dockerfile, the Jenkinsfile, the Kubernetes manifests (Deployment, Service, Ingress, ConfigMap/Secret), and a screenshot or export of the dashboard. Write a one-page runbook answering: where does a failed security scan stop the flow, and what does the readiness probe protect during a rollout? This is the portfolio artifact that proves the whole module — each tool demonstrated by a running system, not by notes.

modules.title: Cloud-Native: The Kubernetes Certification Stack
modules.summary: Welcome back to IL-05 — Cloud DevSecOps Platform SRE. I'm your instructor, and this is Module 2: the Kubernetes certification stack — KCNA to CKA to CKAD to CKS. We'll climb the ladder in order: the architecture and etcd fundamentals of the KCNA/CKA tier, workloads and scheduling, services and networking, storage and the troubleshooting discipline that the CKA secretly grades; the developer-facing CKAD skills of probes, rollouts, and config; and the CKS security tier — cluster hardening, supply-chain security with image signing, and runtime defense with Falco, seccomp, and AppArmor. Every one of these exams is performance-based and practiced in live clusters, so we drill the kubectl speed that the format rewards.
objectives: Explain Kubernetes architecture: API server, scheduler, controller manager, etcd, kubelet.
Schedule and troubleshoot workloads: deployments, statefulsets, daemonsets, jobs.
Configure services, ingress, network policies, and persistent storage.
Harden clusters: RBAC, pod security, image supply chain, runtime policies.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
The certification-stack vocabulary — KCNA terms first, then the CKA/CKAD/CKS depth.
- **control plane** — the cluster brain: API server, scheduler, controller manager, etcd.
- **kubelet** — the node agent that runs pods as the control plane instructs.
- **etcd** — the cluster's source of truth; all state lives here. Back it up with `etcdctl snapshot save`.
- **resource request** — the scheduling guarantee; the scheduler places pods by requests.
- **resource limit** — the enforcement ceiling; CPU throttles, memory kills (OOMKilled).
- **taint / toleration** — taints repel pods from nodes; tolerations let specific pods schedule anyway.
- **affinity** — scheduling preference rules (node or pod affinity/anti-affinity).
- **ClusterIP / NodePort / LoadBalancer** — the service types: internal-only, node-port exposure, cloud load balancer.
- **CNI** — the container network interface layer; know it at concept level for CKA.
- **PV / PVC** — persistent volume (the storage) and persistent volume claim (the request); StorageClasses provision dynamically.
- **init container** — runs to completion before app containers start; the CKAD setup hook.
- **liveness probe** — restarts the container when it fails.
- **readiness probe** — removes the pod from service endpoints when it fails; no restart.
- **startup probe** — guards slow starters so liveness doesn't kill them mid-boot.
- **Pod Security Standards** — privileged, baseline, restricted; each level forbids more.
- **admission control** — the policy enforcement point where supply-chain rules actually bite.
- **cosign** — image signing; signed images plus admission enforcement is the supply-chain gate.
- **Falco** — runtime threat detection on syscalls; detects anomalous behavior in running containers.
- **seccomp** — syscall filtering profiles that constrain what a compromised container can invoke.
- **AppArmor** — mandatory access control profiles constraining process capabilities.
- **KCSA** — the associate-level cloud-native security exam; the on-ramp before CKS.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Drill the exact motions the performance exams grade: speed, triage order, and backup discipline.
1. **Generate, don't hand-write.** Build manifests imperatively: `kubectl create deploy web --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > deploy.yaml`, then `kubectl expose deploy web --port=80 --dry-run=client -o yaml >> deploy.yaml`. Aliases and `--dry-run=client -o yaml` are the exam skill.
2. **Triage in fixed order.** Break a cluster, then fix it the same way every time: `kubectl describe` the object, `kubectl logs` the container, read events, then check the kubelet. Troubleshooting is the CKA's largest hidden domain.
3. **Back up etcd.** Run `etcdctl snapshot save` with the right flags against a test cluster, then practice the restore — the restore is the tested skill.
4. **Probe lab.** Deploy an app with misconfigured liveness and readiness probes; observe the restart loop versus the traffic blackhole, then fix each. Misconfigured probes are the #1 self-inflicted outage.
5. **Harden.** Apply a restricted Pod Security Standard, add a seccomp profile, write a Falco rule alerting on an unexpected shell in a container, and require signed images at admission with an ImagePolicyWebhook-style gate.
notes.code:
# Imperative speed: generate YAML, don't hand-write it
kubectl create deploy web --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > deploy.yaml
kubectl expose deploy web --port=80 --dry-run=client -o yaml >> deploy.yaml
kubectl set image deploy/web web=nginx:1.27  # rollout
kubectl rollout status deploy/web

# Triage order: describe -> logs -> events -> kubelet
kubectl describe pod <pod>
kubectl logs <pod> --previous
kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp

# etcd backup (know the flags; restore is the tested skill)
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /tmp/etcd-backup.db \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key

notes.body: Build the 'broken cluster' lab and its runbook: provision a test cluster, inject five faults (bad image, failed probe, resource exhaustion, bad network policy, corrupted etcd member — with a snapshot taken first), and fix each using the fixed triage order, timing yourself. Deliverables: the fault-injection script or checklist, the triage runbook (describe → logs → events → kubelet), and a hardening checklist applied afterward (restricted PSS, seccomp, one Falco rule, signed-image admission). This is the CKA/CKS muscle memory — speed with kubectl under a 2-hour clock, with docs allowed.

modules.title: Zero-Trust Platform Architecture
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 3 of IL-05 — Cloud DevSecOps Platform SRE. I'm your instructor, and this module turns NIST SP 800-207 into a platform blueprint you can actually build. We'll walk the seven tenets, the policy engine / policy administrator / policy enforcement point, and the control-plane-versus-data-plane split; rebuild the perimeter around identity with phishing-resistant MFA, device posture, continuous authentication, and privileged access; design microsegmentation for the east-west traffic where lateral movement lives; and compare the three deployment models before sequencing a real migration from perimeter security. The exam tests the models; the job tests the patience — we prepare you for both.
objectives: State the seven zero-trust tenets and map them to controls.
Design identity-first access: phishing-resistant MFA, device posture, continuous auth.
Plan microsegmentation: east-west inspection, software-defined perimeters, encrypted everything.
Choose a deployment model and sequence migration from perimeter security.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
The SP 800-207 vocabulary, exactly as the tenets and components define it.
- **zero trust** — 'never trust, always verify'; access granted per session to least privilege, never by network location.
- **tenet 1** — all data sources and services are resources.
- **tenet 2** — all communication is secured regardless of network location.
- **tenet 3** — access to resources is granted on a per-session basis.
- **tenet 4** — access is determined by dynamic policy: identity, device, and behavior.
- **tenet 5** — the enterprise monitors the integrity and security posture of all assets.
- **tenet 6** — authentication and authorization are dynamic and strictly enforced before access.
- **tenet 7** — the enterprise collects maximum information to improve its security posture.
- **Policy Engine (PE)** — the component that decides: evaluates policy and the trust algorithm.
- **Policy Administrator (PA)** — the component that executes: provisions credentials and configures the PEP.
- **Policy Enforcement Point (PEP)** — the gate where the decision is enforced: gateway, agent, or enclave.
- **trust algorithm** — the PE's decision logic: static rules versus dynamic behavioral scoring; policy logic, not ML magic.
- **control plane** — where policy decisions are made; separated from the data plane.
- **data plane** — where the traffic actually flows.
- **phishing-resistant MFA** — FIDO2/WebAuthn: cryptographic, origin-bound authentication. The MFA strength ladder is FIDO2 > TOTP app > SMS (SIM-swappable) > none.
- **device posture** — managed, patched, encrypted, EDR-healthy; a policy input that automatically reduces access for unhealthy devices.
- **continuous authentication** — re-verification on risk signals, not just at login.
- **privileged access workstation (PAW)** — hardened admin tiering; never administer the kingdom from a browsing laptop.
- **microsegmentation** — workload-to-workload policy on east-west traffic.
- **software-defined perimeter (SDP)** — authenticate first, connect second; the network is dark until identity and posture verify.
- **east-west traffic** — internal workload-to-workload traffic; the lateral-movement surface.
- **north-south traffic** — traffic entering or leaving the perimeter.
- **device agent/gateway model** — a deployment model with an agent or gateway as the PEP.
- **enclave model** — a deployment model with per-resource (or per-group) PEPs.
- **resource portal model** — a deployment model with a gateway fronting legacy resources.
- **CISA zero-trust maturity model** — traditional → advanced → optimal, across pillars.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Turn the tenets into an architecture review you can run on any estate. Work it as a procedure, not a slogan.
1. **Inventory and classify.** List resources and data flows; rank by value. Migration starts at the crown jewels — inventory and classification are step one, always.
2. **Draw the decision path.** For one critical resource, diagram subject → PEP → PA/PE: where is the enforcement point, what does the trust algorithm evaluate (identity, device posture, behavior), and what does the PA configure on grant?
3. **Identity-first access design.** Specify the MFA ladder per tier (FIDO2 for privileged and high-value, TOTP minimum elsewhere), device-posture inputs, and just-in-time privileged elevation with session recording.
4. **Microsegment one flow.** Write the east-west policy for a single workload pair (allow only the required ports/protocols, default deny), and require mTLS between the services.
5. **Pick the deployment model.** Match agent/gateway, enclave, or resource portal to the resource's constraints (managed devices? legacy app? per-resource sensitivity?) and justify the PEP placement.
6. **Measure.** Define the migration metrics before starting: % of access decisions via PE/PEP, % phishing-resistant MFA enrollment, mean time to grant/revoke, and lateral-movement test results.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Produce the zero-trust migration plan for a fictional 500-person company with one legacy datacenter app and a growing SaaS footprint. Deliverables: the tenet-to-control map (each of the seven tenets mapped to concrete controls), the PE/PA/PEP diagram for the highest-value resource, the identity design (MFA ladder, device posture, privileged access), one microsegmentation policy, the chosen deployment model with PEP-placement rationale, and the phased migration sequence (inventory → classify → pilot → expand) with the CISA maturity steps marked. Grade it on rationale: two good architects can disagree on the model, but both must defend the fit.

modules.summary: Welcome to Module 4 of IL-05 — Cloud DevSecOps Platform SRE. I'm your instructor, and this module is HashiCorp Terraform through the Associate (003) exam. We'll write HCL the way the exam thinks — resources, providers, data sources, variables, outputs, locals — then run the core workflow until it's reflex: init, validate, plan, apply, destroy. State is the crown jewels, so we give it the full treatment: remote backends, locking, import, and refactoring moves. Then module composition, workspaces, and the Associate exam's domain map with exam-day logistics. The exam loves 'what happens when' — we reason every answer from the state model, not from memorization.
objectives: Write HCL: resources, data sources, variables, outputs, locals.
Run the workflow: init → validate → plan → apply → destroy.
Manage state: remote backends, locking, import, refactoring moves.
Compose modules; use workspaces; pass the Terraform Associate exam.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
The HCL and state vocabulary the Associate exam is built on.
- **resource** — a `resource "aws_instance" "web"` block declaring desired state.
- **provider** — the plugin that talks to an API (AWS, Azure, and others).
- **data source** — reads existing infrastructure into config; the brownfield bridge.
- **variable / output / local** — the parameterization trio: inputs, exposed values, internal expressions.
- **init** — installs providers and modules; the workflow's first step.
- **validate** — checks syntax and internal consistency.
- **plan** — computes the diff; the code review of infrastructure. Read it — never auto-apply blind in production.
- **apply** — executes the planned changes.
- **state** — the mapping of config to real resources; lose it and Terraform forgets your infrastructure.
- **remote state** — shared, locked, versioned state (S3 + DynamoDB/S3-native locking, Terraform Cloud, GCS).
- **state locking** — serializes applies; concurrent applies without locking corrupt state.
- **import** — `terraform import aws_instance.web i-12345` binds brownfield to state; you must then write matching config.
- **moved block** — refactors resources (rename, module shift) without destroy/recreate.
- **drift** — real infrastructure diverging from config; apply converges it after you review the plan.
- **taint / replace** — marks a resource for recreation.
- **module** — a composable unit: root module calls child modules via `source`; inputs via variables, outputs bubble up.
- **workspace** — `terraform workspace new prod`: same config, separate states; fine for small setups, separate configs for serious multi-env.
- **count vs for_each** — count for identical numbered instances (fragile: removing the middle shifts indices and recreates); for_each for named instances with stable keys.
- **remote state data source** — shares outputs between configurations; composition over duplication.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run the workflow the way production demands: plan as code review, state as crown jewels.
1. **Init and validate.** `terraform init`, then `terraform validate` — providers installed, syntax clean.
2. **Plan to a file.** `terraform plan -out=tfplan`; read the diff like a code review: every create/update/destroy must be intentional. The saved plan is the auditable artifact.
3. **Apply the saved plan.** `terraform apply tfplan` — never `apply` without the reviewed plan in production.
4. **Remote state with locking.** Configure the backend (S3 + DynamoDB/S3-native locking or Terraform Cloud) so concurrent applies serialize instead of corrupting state. Never hand-edit state except via `terraform state mv`/`rm` — and back it up first.
5. **Import brownfield.** `terraform import` the existing resource, then write the matching config immediately — import only binds state; the config must describe it.
6. **Refactor safely.** Use `moved` blocks to rename or shift modules without destroy/recreate; run `terraform fmt` and `validate` in CI like app code.
7. **Compose.** Split a VPC + compute stack into child modules with clear inputs/outputs; share outputs between configurations via the remote state data source.
notes.code:
# The disciplined workflow: plan to a file, review, then apply
terraform init
terraform validate
terraform fmt -check
terraform plan -out=tfplan     # READ THE DIFF — the code review of infra
terraform apply tfplan        # apply the reviewed plan, never blind

# Remote state with locking (the crown jewels, protected)
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket         = "tf-state-prod"
    key            = "network/terraform.tfstate"
    region         = "us-east-1"
    dynamodb_table = "tf-state-locks"
    encrypt        = true
  }
}

# Brownfield: import first, then write the matching config
terraform import aws_instance.web i-12345

# Refactor without destroy/recreate
moved {
  from = aws_instance.web
  to   = module.compute.aws_instance.web
}

modules.title: AWS Solutions Architecture: SAA-C03
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 5 of IL-05 — Cloud DevSecOps Platform SRE. I'm your instructor, and we now drive the AWS certification spine, starting with the Solutions Architect Associate (SAA-C03). We'll design for failure with multi-AZ resilience and decoupled components; choose compute, storage, and databases by workload shape and cache at every layer; secure applications with IAM, KMS, security groups versus NACLs, and WAF; and optimize cost across pricing models, S3 tiers, and right-sizing. Along the way we build the Terraform reference stacks — composable VPC, ALB+ASG, RDS, and S3+CloudFront modules — so every architecture here is also infrastructure as code. SAA scenarios always hide two plausible answers; we train the constraint-first elimination the exam rewards.
objectives: Design multi-AZ resilient architectures with decoupled components.
Select compute/storage/database services by workload requirements.
Apply IAM, encryption, and network security to architectures.
Optimize cost: pricing models, storage tiers, and right-sizing.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
The architect's vocabulary — the four SAA pillars in glossary form.
- **Availability Zone (AZ)** — an isolated failure domain; multi-AZ (not just multi-instance) is the resilience unit.
- **decoupling** — SQS/SNS/EventBridge between tiers; turns cascading failures into queue depth, because a failed consumer retries instead of a failed request erroring.
- **RTO / RPO** — recovery time / recovery point objectives; the business numbers that choose the DR pattern.
- **DR patterns** — backup-restore → pilot light → warm standby → multi-site active-active; cost and recovery speed rise together.
- **ALB** — application load balancer, spread across AZs.
- **RDS Multi-AZ** — standby replica in another AZ for failover.
- **S3 durability** — the 11-9s design target.
- **compute selection** — EC2 vs Lambda vs Fargate vs ECS, chosen by workload shape.
- **storage selection** — EBS gp3/io2, EFS, S3, instance store, chosen by access pattern.
- **Aurora** — the relational choice for complex joins and transactions.
- **DynamoDB** — the key-value choice at scale.
- **caching** — CloudFront and ElastiCache; cache at every layer.
- **elasticity** — Auto Scaling on the right metric.
- **security group** — stateful, instance-level; return traffic is allowed automatically.
- **NACL** — stateless, subnet-level; explicit rules in both directions — the classic exam trap.
- **KMS** — envelope encryption with customer-managed keys (CMKs).
- **permission boundary** — caps the maximum permissions a delegated identity can get.
- **WAF / Shield** — web-application firewall and DDoS protection.
- **pricing models** — On-Demand vs Reserved vs Spot vs Savings Plans, chosen by workload steadiness.
- **S3 tiers** — Standard → Intelligent-Tiering → Glacier, chosen by access recency; Intelligent-Tiering auto-optimizes unpredictable patterns.
- **right-sizing** — Compute Optimizer-driven instance fit; data transfer awareness (same-AZ free, cross-region metered).

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Design like the exam grades: constraints first, then services.
1. **State RTO/RPO.** Write the business numbers down first; they choose the DR pattern (backup-restore through multi-site active).
2. **Multi-AZ every tier.** Place the ALB across AZs and the instances across AZs too — an ALB in 2 AZs with instances in 1 AZ is not resilient.
3. **Decouple.** Put SQS between any two tiers where a slowdown must not cascade; monitor queue depth, not just the app.
4. **Choose by pattern.** Database: complex joins → Aurora; key-value at scale → DynamoDB. Compute and storage by workload shape and access pattern.
5. **Secure the layers.** Least-privilege IAM (roles, not users, for apps), KMS envelope encryption, security groups for stateful instance rules and NACLs with explicit both-direction rules at the subnet.
6. **Cost it.** Baseline on Savings Plans/Reserved, peaks on On-Demand/Spot; tier S3 by access recency; set TTLs and versioned keys for cache invalidation.
7. **Codify.** Express the design as the Terraform reference stacks: VPC, ALB+ASG, RDS, S3+CloudFront as composable modules.
8. **Eliminate by constraint.** On scenario questions with two plausible answers, re-read for the deciding constraint — cost, resilience, or ops overhead — and let it pick.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Design a three-tier web application for a fictional retailer: state the RTO/RPO, draw the multi-AZ architecture with a decoupled order pipeline (SQS between web and fulfillment), justify the database choice by query pattern, apply the security layering (IAM roles, KMS, SG vs NACL), and cost the steady baseline plus spiky peaks across pricing models. Deliverables: the architecture diagram, the constraint log (every major choice tied to cost, resilience, or ops overhead), and the Terraform reference-stack modules (VPC, ALB+ASG, RDS, S3+CloudFront). This is the SAA muscle: defend the trade-offs, not just the choices.

modules.title: AWS CloudOps: SysOps Administrator
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 6 of IL-05 — Cloud DevSecOps Platform SRE. I'm your instructor, and this module is the operator's exam: the AWS Certified SysOps Administrator Associate. We'll provision with CloudFormation and ship blue/green deployments whose rollback story is the feature; design reliability and business continuity around backups, multi-AZ patterns, and Route 53 failover; run security and compliance operations with CloudTrail, Config, IAM Access Analyzer, and GuardDuty; and master the networking and cost/performance domains — VPC endpoints, CloudFront, right-sizing, and Graviton. The SysOps exam is scenario-dense: every domain is a runbook, so we drill monitor → detect → respond until it's reflex.
objectives: Provision with CloudFormation and run blue/green deployments.
Design backup/DR to RTO/RPO with AWS Backup and multi-AZ patterns.
Operate securely: CloudTrail, Config, IAM Access Analyzer, GuardDuty.
Optimize: Cost Explorer, Compute Optimizer, S3 lifecycle, CloudFront caching.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
The operator's glossary — every pair the exam loves to test.
- **CloudFormation** — declarative infrastructure stacks; drift detection finds the console cowboys; StackSets extend to multi-account.
- **blue/green deployment** — CodeDeploy shifts traffic between environments; the rollback story is the feature.
- **Systems Manager** — Patch Manager, Run Command, Parameter Store: the operator's console.
- **golden AMI** — baked, tested, distributed images via EC2 Image Builder; immutable infrastructure starts here.
- **AWS Backup** — centralized backup policies with cross-region copy.
- **Route 53 health checks + failover routing** — DNS steers away from the dead region.
- **CloudTrail** — who did what: the API-activity audit log.
- **Config** — what changed: resource state over time, with rules and remediation. The exam pairs Trail and Config constantly.
- **IAM Access Analyzer** — finds unintended, over-permissive access; the least-privilege auditor.
- **GuardDuty** — threat detection on the logs; findings feed EventBridge → Lambda/SSM for the automated response loop.
- **Security Hub** — the aggregated security posture view.
- **VPC Gateway endpoint** — S3/DynamoDB access off the internet; free, via a route-table entry.
- **VPC Interface endpoint** — PrivateLink-powered access to other services; hourly charge.
- **CloudFront signed URLs/cookies + OAC** — private content delivered through the CDN with authorized access.
- **routing policies** — failover, latency-based, geoproximity: the Route 53 traffic shapes.
- **Cost Explorer + Budgets** — spend visibility and guardrails.
- **Compute Optimizer** — right-sizing recommendations.
- **S3 lifecycle policies** — automatic tiering and expiry by age.
- **gp3 over gp2** — cheaper and independently tunable.
- **Graviton** — the price-performance processor option.
- **untested backup** — a rumor; the RTO is only real if restores are proven on schedule.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Operate it like the exam's scenarios: deploy, back up, detect drift, respond.
1. **Deploy blue/green.** Ship a CodeDeploy blue/green deployment; rehearse the rollback — the rollback story is the feature, and deploying without one is a hope.
2. **Bake a golden AMI.** Use EC2 Image Builder to bake, test, and distribute an AMI; deploy from it so infrastructure stays immutable.
3. **Back up to RTO/RPO.** Create an AWS Backup plan with cross-region copy, then actually test a restore — untested backups are rumors.
4. **Wire the response loop.** Enable GuardDuty, route findings through EventBridge to a Lambda/SSM Automation remediation — detect to remediate without humans in the path.
5. **Find the cowboys.** Run CloudFormation drift detection on a stack someone touched in the console; import or revert deliberately.
6. **Audit access.** Run IAM Access Analyzer and remediate one over-permissive grant toward least privilege.
7. **Cut the transfer bill.** Replace NAT-gateway S3 traffic with a Gateway VPC endpoint; serve private media via CloudFront signed URLs with Origin Access Control.

# Gateway VPC endpoint: S3 traffic stays on the AWS network (free)
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint \
  --vpc-id vpc-12345678 \
  --service-name com.amazonaws.us-east-1.s3 \
  --route-table-ids rtb-abcdef12

# Drift detection: find the console cowboys
aws cloudformation detect-stack-drift --stack-name web-prod
aws cloudformation describe-stack-resource-drifts --stack-name web-prod

# Who did what: recent API activity via CloudTrail lookup
aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=ConsoleLogin

modules.title: AWS DevOps Professional: DOP-C02
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 7 of IL-05 — Cloud DevSecOps Platform SRE. I'm your instructor, and we now climb to the professional tier: the AWS Certified DevOps Engineer Professional (DOP-C02). We'll automate the SDLC with CodePipeline, canary and linear deployments, and feature flags that decouple deploy from release; manage IaC at scale with nested stacks, StackSets, and drift governance; design resilient multi-region solutions with honest data-replication thinking and chaos experiments; trace systems with CloudWatch Logs Insights and X-Ray; and run incident response and pipeline security — signed artifacts, scanning gates, least-privilege pipeline roles. It's the longest exam at 180 minutes of scenarios; we train the pace and the constraint-first elimination it demands.
objectives: Build SDLC automation: pipelines, deployment strategies, automated rollbacks.
Manage IaC at scale: nested stacks, StackSets, drift governance.
Design multi-region resilience with data replication realities.
Trace and respond: X-Ray, Logs Insights, EventBridge-driven remediation.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
The professional-tier vocabulary.
- **CodePipeline** — the AWS SDLC automation service: source → build → deploy stages.
- **canary deployment** — release in percentage steps (10% → 50% → 100%) with metric gates and automatic rollback on regression.
- **linear deployment** — release a fixed percentage every N minutes.
- **all-at-once deployment** — fastest, riskiest; no safety net.
- **feature flag** — decouples deploy from release; the safest deployment is the one you can turn off without redeploying.
- **nested stack** — CloudFormation composition: stacks calling stacks.
- **StackSet** — one template deployed across N accounts and regions; the org-scale deployment primitive and the landing-zone tool.
- **drift governance** — detecting and reconciling template-vs-reality drift at scale.
- **active-active multi-region** — Route 53 plus replicated data; compute is the easy part, data replication is the hard part.
- **chaos thinking / Fault Injection Simulator (FIS)** — prove resilience with injected failures; resilience is proven, not asserted.
- **CloudWatch composite alarm** — alarms on the AND of symptoms; reduces noise versus alarming on each symptom.
- **Logs Insights** — query language over CloudWatch Logs (e.g. filter @message like /ERROR/).
- **X-Ray** — distributed tracing; the service map draws itself — start every latency hunt there.
- **SSM Automation document** — the executable runbook; incident response as code.
- **artifact signing** — CodeSigner/signer Lambda provenance: deploy only signed artifacts; unsigned artifacts don't deploy.
- **pipeline IAM role** — the pipeline's identity is a blast radius; scope it with least privilege to exactly the deploy actions.
- **blameless post-incident review** — fix the system, not the person.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Ship the professional way: gated rollouts, traced systems, signed artifacts.
1. **Pipeline.** Build a CodePipeline (source → build → deploy) with a scanning gate before the deploy stage — SAST, dependency, and container scans.
2. **Canary.** Deploy with a canary strategy (10% → 50% → 100%), gating each step on canary-vs-baseline error rate and latency with automatic rollback on regression.
3. **Flag it.** Wrap the new feature in a feature flag so a bad release is mitigated by flipping the flag — no redeploy.
4. **Scale the IaC.** Convert the stack to nested stacks, then deploy it across two regions with a StackSet.
5. **Trace.** Instrument with X-Ray; open the service map and run one Logs Insights query to find the slow dependency.
6. **Game day.** Run a Fault Injection Simulator experiment against the multi-region setup and record what actually failed over.
7. **Sign.** Add artifact signing to the pipeline; verify an unsigned artifact is rejected at the deploy stage.
8. **Pace.** Drill 180-minute scenario blocks: eliminate by constraint, flag the 50/50s, keep moving.

# Logs Insights: find the errors fast
fields @timestamp, @message
| filter @message like /ERROR/
| stats count() by bin(5m)

# X-Ray: trace a request through 40 microservices
aws xray get-trace-summaries \
  --start-time $(date -u -d '1 hour ago' +%s) \
  --end-time $(date -u +%s) \
  --filter-expression 'service("checkout-api") { error = true }'

Deliverables: the pipeline definition, the canary/rollback runbook, the game-day findings, and a pacing plan for the 180-minute exam. modules.title: AWS Security Specialty: SCS-C03
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 8 of IL-05 — Cloud DevSecOps Platform SRE. I'm your instructor, and this is the security specialty: the AWS Certified Security Specialty (SCS-C03). We'll detect and respond with GuardDuty, Detective, Security Hub, and Macie; log everything with org-wide CloudTrail, Config aggregators, and Athena forensics; lock IAM down with permission boundaries, SCPs, ABAC, and cross-account roles; protect data with KMS envelope encryption and hardened S3; and assemble the hardened landing zone — Control Tower with preventive and detective guardrails. The landing zone is the exam's favorite scenario: a new org, secure by default, compliant by construction.
objectives: Detect and respond: GuardDuty → Detective → automated containment.
Log everything: org CloudTrail, Config aggregation, Athena analysis.
Lock IAM: boundaries, SCPs, ABAC, cross-account patterns.
Protect data: KMS envelope encryption, S3 protections, Macie.
Build the hardened landing zone with preventive + detective guardrails.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
The specialty's glossary — detection, identity, data, and the landing zone.
- **GuardDuty** — threat detection over the logs; produces findings.
- **Detective** — investigation graphs: pivot from a finding to the entity to the timeline, in clicks not grep marathons.
- **Security Hub** — aggregated security posture across accounts.
- **Macie** — discovers and classifies PII in S3 at scale.
- **org CloudTrail** — the multi-account API audit log; pair with an immutable bucket + Object Lock so attackers can't delete it.
- **Config aggregator** — multi-account resource-state collection for compliance.
- **Athena over CloudTrail** — SQL forensics over the log lake without a SIEM budget.
- **incident response order** — isolate (revoke creds, quarantine security groups), eradicate, recover — with runbooks, not improvisation.
- **permission boundary** — the maximum permissions a delegated admin can grant; caps their power.
- **SCP (service control policy)** — org-level guardrail; bounds even root. SCPs restrict — they never grant.
- **ABAC** — attribute-based access control: tag principals and resources, write one policy; scales where RBAC explodes.
- **cross-account role** — temporary credentials for partner/third-party access; no long-lived keys, no rotation burden.
- **WAF** — managed rules plus rate limiting; rate-based rules stop brute-force and scraping floods.
- **Shield Advanced** — managed DDoS protection.
- **Network Firewall** — VPC-level stateful inspection.
- **PrivateLink** — access AWS services and partner services without traversing the internet.
- **KMS envelope encryption** — the data key (DEK) encrypts the data; the KMS master key (KEK) encrypts the DEK — scale without KMS throttling.
- **S3 Block Public Access** — set at the account level first; bucket policies are then defense in depth.
- **S3 Object Lock** — immutability for compliance and log protection.
- **Control Tower** — the account factory plus guardrails: the hardened landing zone.
- **preventive guardrail** — SCPs (deny unencrypted S3, deny wrong regions): stops the bad action.
- **detective guardrail** — Config rules and Security Hub findings: catches what slipped through.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Build the secure-by-default org, then prove you can investigate inside it.
1. **Org trail.** Enable an org-wide CloudTrail into a dedicated log account with Object Lock on the bucket — the audit log attackers can't delete.
2. **Aggregate.** Turn on the Config aggregator and Security Hub across the org; note one finding end to end.
3. **Guardrails.** Apply preventive SCPs (deny unencrypted S3, deny deployments outside approved regions) and one detective Config rule; verify a violating action is blocked, not just flagged.
4. **IAM depth.** Create a delegated admin with a permission boundary; write one ABAC policy using principal tags; grant a partner temporary access via a cross-account role — no access keys.
5. **Data.** Enable account-level S3 Block Public Access; encrypt a bucket with a customer-managed KMS key (envelope encryption in action); run Macie on a test bucket.
6. **Investigate.** Take a GuardDuty finding, pivot through Detective's graph to the root cause, and query the org trail with Athena for the full timeline.
7. **Respond.** Execute the isolate → eradicate → recover runbook on a simulated compromised credential: revoke, quarantine the security group, rotate.

modules.title: Azure Administration: The AZ-104 Spine
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 9 of IL-05 — Cloud DevSecOps Platform SRE. I'm your instructor, and we cross to the Azure spine, starting with administration: the AZ-104. We'll run Entra ID and RBAC — users, groups, devices, licenses, roles, scopes, least privilege, and PIM for just-in-time elevation; govern with management groups, Azure Policy, locks, and tagging; operate storage accounts with tiers, redundancy, and lifecycle management; run compute from VMs and VMSS to containers; build virtual networks with NSGs, peering, and Private Endpoints; and close with monitoring, backup, and recovery. Identity is the control plane and the exam's heaviest domain — we lab every objective on a real subscription.
objectives: Administer Entra ID: users, groups, devices, licenses, PIM.
Apply RBAC: built-in/custom roles, scopes, least privilege.
Govern: management groups, policy, locks, tags.
Run storage, compute, networking, and Monitor/backup/recovery.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
The AZ-104 glossary — identity first, then the platform.
- **Entra ID** — the identity plane: users, groups (security vs Microsoft 365), devices (join/register), licenses.
- **RBAC** — role-based access: Owner/Contributor/Reader plus granular roles; who can do what.
- **RBAC scope** — management group → subscription → resource group → resource; assignments inherit downward.
- **least privilege** — the standing rule for every assignment.
- **PIM (Privileged Identity Management)** — just-in-time elevation: eligible assignments with approval, time-bound. Standing admin is the vulnerability.
- **management group** — the hierarchy above subscriptions; assign policy and RBAC once, inherit everywhere.
- **Azure Policy** — compliance as code: deny, audit, deployIfNotExists effects; governs what configurations are allowed.
- **resource lock** — CanNotDelete / ReadOnly; CanNotDelete on production resource groups is the cheapest outage insurance.
- **storage tiers** — Hot / Cool / Cold / Archive; cost follows access recency.
- **redundancy ladder** — LRS (3 copies, 1 datacenter) → ZRS (3 zones) → GRS (+ paired region) → RA-GRS; durability and cost rise together.
- **lifecycle management** — rules that tier aging blobs down automatically; storage cost is a policy, not a hope.
- **SAS vs keys** — shared access signatures (scoped, expiring) versus storage account keys.
- **availability set vs zone** — sets survive rack loss; zones survive datacenter loss. Zones are the resilience default.
- **VMSS** — virtual machine scale sets: autoscaling VM fleets.
- **NSG** — network security group: lowest rule number wins; defaults deny inbound internet.
- **peering** — VNet peering; transit goes via the hub.
- **Private Endpoint** — PaaS services (Storage, SQL) get VNet-private IPs; off the public internet.
- **Load Balancer** — L4 regional distribution.
- **Application Gateway** — L7 with WAF and path/host routing.
- **Azure Monitor / Log Analytics** — metrics and logs; KQL queries over the workspace.
- **Recovery Services vault** — Azure Backup policies and Site Recovery for DR.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Administer a real subscription, identity first.
1. **Kill standing admin.** Move the admin accounts to PIM-eligible assignments with approval and time bounds; verify an elevation request and its audit trail.
2. **RBAC by scope.** Create a custom role with least privilege, assign it at the resource-group scope, and confirm inheritance blocks at the subscription level.
3. **Govern once.** Build the management-group hierarchy, assign an Azure Policy initiative (e.g. deny public storage) at the top, and confirm a violating deployment is denied.
4. **Lock production.** Apply CanNotDelete locks to the production resource groups; attempt a delete and watch it fail safely.
5. **Tier the storage.** Create a storage account, write a lifecycle rule (Hot → Cool → Archive by age), and compare the redundancy options on the durability/cost ladder.
6. **Zone the compute.** Deploy across availability zones (not sets); put a VMSS behind the load balancer with autoscale.
7. **Private the PaaS.** Add a Private Endpoint to the storage account; verify traffic no longer needs the public endpoint.
8. **Query.** Learn five KQL queries against Log Analytics (CPU spikes, failed sign-ins, and three of your choosing) and save them; set one alert with an action group.
notes.code:
# KQL: CPU spikes over 5-minute windows
AzureMetrics
| where MetricName has 'Percentage CPU'
| summarize avg(Average) by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m), Resource
| where avg_Average > 80

# KQL: failed sign-ins (identity is the control plane — watch it)
SigninLogs
| where ResultType != 0
| summarize count() by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| order by count_ desc

modules.title: Azure Solutions Architecture: AZ-305
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 10 of IL-05 — Cloud DevSecOps Platform SRE. I'm your instructor, and we shift from administering Azure to designing it: the AZ-305. We'll design identity, governance, and monitoring for a multi-subscription enterprise; choose data services by workload pattern — Azure SQL, Cosmos DB with its five consistency levels, Storage, and the analytics tier; design business continuity where RTO/RPO choose between backup and Site Recovery; and design infrastructure across compute, network, and migrations. It all caps in the architecture capstone: a full design with documented trade-offs, graded on rationale — two good architects can disagree, but both must defend.
objectives: Design identity/governance for a multi-subscription enterprise.
Choose data services by workload pattern: relational, NoSQL, analytical.
Design business continuity to RTO/RPO with Site Recovery and backup.
Produce a full architecture with documented trade-offs (the capstone).

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
The architect's design vocabulary.
- **landing zone** — the enterprise scaffold: platform subscriptions plus workload subscriptions under management groups, governed centrally.
- **hybrid identity** — Entra Connect sync versus federation; B2B/B2C for external identity shapes.
- **Access Reviews** — recurring, auditable certification of access; governance that doesn't rot.
- **policy initiative** — bundled policies assigned at the management group for org-wide compliance.
- **Log Analytics workspace strategy** — central versus regional workspaces; alert routing and workbooks for the business view.
- **Azure SQL** — the relational, familiar choice.
- **Cosmos DB** — global NoSQL with five consistency levels: Strong → Bounded Staleness → Session → Consistent Prefix → Eventual; latency and availability trade per level.
- **hot/warm/cold path** — stream (Event Hubs) → serve (Cosmos DB) → analyze (Synapse): the lambda/kappa shapes.
- **backup vs Site Recovery** — backup: RPO-hours, cheap. Site Recovery: replication with failover runbooks, RPO-minutes, for tier-1 workloads. The numbers choose.
- **compute selection** — App Service vs AKS vs VMs vs Functions, chosen by workload shape.
- **hub-spoke** — shared services in the hub (firewall, DNS, VPN), workloads in spokes; peering is non-transitive by default, so spoke-to-spoke routes via the hub.
- **ExpressRoute vs VPN** — dedicated private circuit versus internet VPN; the SLA and consistency need decides.
- **Azure Migrate** — assess → replicate → test cutover → cutover; migrations run in waves, never big-bang.
- **design grading criterion** — rationale fit to constraints; defend the trade-offs, not just the choices.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Design in the order the exam asks: identity, data, continuity, infrastructure — then defend it.
1. **Identity design.** Sketch the tenant shape (single vs B2B/B2C), hybrid approach (sync vs federation), and the PIM + Access Reviews governance loop.
2. **Governance design.** Draw the management-group hierarchy (platform vs workload subscriptions), the policy initiatives, and the tagging + cost-management strategy.
3. **Data design.** For each workload, pick by pattern: relational → Azure SQL; global NoSQL with tunable consistency → Cosmos DB (choose the level deliberately); blobs/files/queues/tables → Storage by pattern; analytics → Synapse/Fabric.
4. **Continuity design.** Write the RTO/RPO per tier; assign backup (RPO-hours) or Site Recovery (RPO-minutes) accordingly — the numbers choose the tool.
5. **Infrastructure design.** Select compute by workload, draw hub-spoke with the firewall and gateway in the hub, and plan the migration in waves with Azure Migrate.
6. **Monitoring design.** Choose the workspace strategy (central vs regional), alert routing, and the workbooks the business will actually read.
7. **Trade-off log.** For every major choice, record the constraint it serves (compliance? cost? operability?) and the rejected alternative — the exam grades the fit.

modules.title: Azure Network Engineering: AZ-700
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 11 of IL-05 — Cloud DevSecOps Platform SRE. I'm your instructor, and this is the network specialist's module: the AZ-700. We'll build the core networking infrastructure — VNets, subnets, NSGs, peering, private DNS — with address planning done once and done right; connect with VPN Gateway, ExpressRoute, and Virtual WAN, picking the SKU by need; deliver applications across the L4/L7/global spectrum — Load Balancer, Application Gateway, Front Door, Traffic Manager; give PaaS private access with Private Link; and secure it all with Azure Firewall, DDoS Protection, and Bastion. The AZ-700 tests selection, not syntax — every scenario asks which service the constraint picks.
objectives: Design VNet topology: addressing, peering, private DNS, NSGs.
Connect: VPN/ExpressRoute/Virtual WAN with the right SKU per need.
Deliver apps: Front Door vs App Gateway vs LB vs Traffic Manager.
Secure: Firewall, DDoS Protection, Bastion, Private Link.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
The network engineer's glossary — selection criteria included.
- **VNet / subnet** — the isolated network and its segments; address space planning is forever — overlapping CIDRs with on-prem break peering and VPN permanently.
- **NSG / ASG** — network security groups (with application security groups for grouping); stateful-ish rules, lowest number wins.
- **peering** — VNet peering; transit via the hub, non-transitive by default.
- **Private DNS zone** — VNet-linked, split-horizon name resolution for private networks.
- **VPN Gateway** — S2S IPsec, P2S, and VNet-to-VNet connectivity over the internet.
- **ExpressRoute** — a private dedicated circuit: consistent latency and throughput with an SLA, not internet variability.
- **Virtual WAN** — Microsoft-managed hub-and-spoke at global scale; global transit without building your own hub mesh.
- **Load Balancer** — L4 regional distribution.
- **Application Gateway** — regional L7 with WAF and path/host routing.
- **Front Door** — global L7 at the edge PoPs with instant failover and WAF; the global web-app answer.
- **Traffic Manager** — DNS-based global routing; failover takes TTL time — not instant like Front Door.
- **Private Link / Private Endpoint** — PaaS services get VNet-private IPs; the strong option for data-exfiltration control.
- **service endpoint** — VNet identity for PaaS access; simpler, but the PaaS stays public-adjacent — weaker than Private Link.
- **Azure Firewall** — L3–L7 filtering with FQDN rules and threat intelligence; egress control that actually works.
- **DDoS Protection** — network-tier protection; enable on the VNet housing public IPs — the attack you can't afford to learn about live.
- **Bastion** — browser-based RDP/SSH with no public IPs; replaces the internet-facing jumpbox — the most-attacked box in the estate.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Design and prove the network in constraint order: address, connect, deliver, secure.
1. **Address once.** Plan non-overlapping CIDRs for hub, spokes, and on-prem; document the scheme — this decision is forever.
2. **Hub-spoke.** Build the hub (firewall, VPN/ExpressRoute gateway, Bastion, Private DNS) and peer the spokes with gateway transit enabled; verify spoke-to-spoke flows through the hub.
3. **Connect.** Stand up the S2S VPN, then compare against the ExpressRoute value proposition (consistent private throughput with SLA) for the workload's need.
4. **Deliver.** Put the regional app behind Application Gateway (L7 + WAF + path routing); put the global app behind Front Door and test the instant failover; note Traffic Manager's TTL-time failover as the DNS-level alternative.
5. **Private the PaaS.** Attach Private Endpoints to Storage and SQL; confirm with service endpoints disabled that exfiltration paths are closed.
6. **Secure.** Write Azure Firewall FQDN rules (allow *.update.microsoft.com, deny the rest); enable DDoS Protection on the public-IP VNet; remove every jumpbox in favor of Bastion.
7. **Select by constraint.** Drill ten scenarios: for each, name the deciding constraint (global? private? L7? instant failover?) and the service it picks — the AZ-700's actual skill.

# Hub-spoke peering with gateway transit (spokes use the hub's VPN/ER gateway)
az network vnet peering create \
  --name spoke-to-hub --resource-group rg-net \
  --vnet-name spoke1 --remote-vnet hub \
  --allow-vnet-access --allow-forwarded-traffic \
  --use-remote-gateways

# Private DNS: VNet-linked resolution for private endpoints
az network private-dns zone create -g rg-net -n privatelink.database.windows.net
az network private-dns link vnet create -g rg-net -z privatelink.database.windows.net \
  -n hub-link --virtual-network hub --registration-enabled false

notes.body:
The OpenShift glossary — admin and dev, side by side.
- **project** — OpenShift's namespace plus membership and annotations; the multitenancy admin boundary.
- **route** — OpenShift's built-in ingress; TLS modes are edge (terminate at the router), passthrough (terminate at the pod), reencrypt (both).
- **S2I (Source-to-Image)** — git push → image → deploy: the developer on-ramp without Dockerfiles.
- **Operator** — cluster extensions as code.
- **IPI / UPI** — installer-provisioned versus user-provisioned installation shapes.
- **quota / limit range** — per-project consumption bounds and defaults; the noisy-neighbor control for multitenancy.
- **OCS/ODF** — the OpenShift storage offerings; StorageClasses for dynamic provisioning.
- **day-2 operations** — upgrades, etcd backup, cert rotation, monitoring: the actual job after the day-1 install.
- **DeploymentConfig** — the OpenShift-native deployment object alongside standard Deployments/StatefulSets.
- **health probe** — liveness/readiness semantics carried into OpenShift deploy patterns.
- **circuit breaker / bulkhead / retry with backoff** — the resilient-microservice patterns, via Service Mesh (Istio) or libraries.
- **Quarkus** — 'supersonic subatomic Java': fast startup, low memory, native images via GraalVM for serverless; dev mode gives live reload — the inner loop that makes Java cloud-credible.
- **twelve-factor** — codebase, dependencies, config (env, not code), backing services (attached resources), build/release/run, stateless processes, port binding, concurrency, disposability, dev/prod parity, logs (event streams), admin processes.
- **container security baseline** — non-root user plus read-only filesystem where possible.

modules.title: Vault & Consul: Secrets and Service Networking
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 13 of IL-05 — Cloud DevSecOps Platform SRE. I'm your instructor, and this module is secrets and service networking: HashiCorp Vault and Consul, through the Vault Associate and Consul Associate exams. We'll run Vault's secrets engines — KV, dynamic database and cloud credentials, PKI, transit — and its auth methods, so humans and machines each authenticate as themselves; write least-privilege policies; and face the operations reality: unseal ceremonies, Raft storage, replication, and monitoring the critical path. Then Consul: the service catalog with DNS and health-checked discovery, and the Connect service mesh with mTLS, intentions, and gateways. Dynamic secrets solve the leaked-credential problem structurally — that idea alone is worth the module.
objectives: Run Vault: engines, auth, policies, unseal/raft operations.
Issue dynamic secrets and manage PKI/transit engines.
Discover services with Consul: catalog, DNS, health checks.
Mesh services: Connect intentions, gateways, mTLS.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
The secrets-and-mesh glossary.
- **KV v2 secrets engine** — versioned static secrets.
- **dynamic secrets** — leased, auto-revoked credentials (database, AWS STS): credentials that expire; the leaked-credential problem solved structurally.
- **PKI secrets engine** — Vault as an internal certificate authority; short-lived certs.
- **transit secrets engine** — encryption-as-a-service: Vault encrypts/decrypts, your data never lands in Vault; crypto without key-management pain.
- **auth method** — how clients prove identity: userpass/LDAP (humans), OIDC (SSO), Kubernetes (pod service accounts), AWS (IAM-based) — machines authenticate as themselves.
- **Vault policy** — HCL paths with capabilities (read, list, create, update, delete, sudo); deny-by-default — nothing is readable until a policy allows it.
- **unseal** — Shamir key shards or auto-unseal via cloud KMS; plan this before production — unseal ceremonies fail at 3 AM otherwise.
- **Raft integrated storage** — Vault's built-in storage backend; no Consul needed anymore. Back it up with `vault operator raft snapshot save`.
- **DR vs performance replication** — disaster-recovery clusters versus read-scaling clusters.
- **Consul catalog** — the registry of services.
- **Consul DNS/HTTP** — `web.service.consul` and the HTTP API: the discovery interfaces.
- **health check gating** — only healthy instances receive traffic; no load-balancer config needed.
- **Consul Connect** — the service mesh: automatic, rotated mTLS between services.
- **intention** — the allow/deny rule for service-to-service traffic (`consul intention create -allow web api`); the firewall rule for services, east-west microsegmentation for the mesh.
- **gateways** — mesh, ingress, and terminating gateways for traffic in and out of the mesh.
- **Consul KV vs Vault** — Consul KV is config, not encrypted by default; secrets belong in Vault.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Stand up secrets and mesh the way production does: unseal planned, policies least-privilege, discovery health-gated.
1. **Init and unseal.** Initialize Vault, then configure auto-unseal via cloud KMS — operators should never handle key shards; rehearse the seal migration and rekey in staging.
2. **Engines.** Enable KV v2 for static secrets, the database engine for dynamic creds, and transit for encryption-as-a-service.
3. **Auth.** Configure OIDC for engineers (SSO) and the Kubernetes auth method for pods — humans via identity provider, machines as themselves.
4. **Policies.** Write deny-by-default policies granting each service only its paths; verify a token can't read outside its policy.
5. **Dynamic rotation.** Issue dynamic database credentials to an app; rotate the lease and confirm the app picks up new creds without restarts.
6. **Raft backup.** Take a Raft snapshot; document the restore.
7. **Consul.** Register services, query `web.service.consul`, add health checks and watch unhealthy instances drain from discovery automatically.
8. **Mesh.** Enable Connect, create the `allow web → api` intention with default deny, and verify mTLS between the services; add a terminating gateway for the legacy dependency.
9. **Monitor the critical path.** Alert on seal status, leader changes, and token-expiry storms — Vault is critical path; watch it like one.
notes.code:
# Dynamic database credentials: leased, auto-rotated, revoked on lease end
vault secrets enable database
vault write database/config/mydb \
  plugin_name=postgresql-database-plugin \
  connection_url="postgresql://{{username}}:{{password}}@db:5432/app" \
  allowed_roles="app"
vault write database/roles/app db_name=mydb \
  creation_statements="CREATE ROLE \"{{name}}\" WITH LOGIN PASSWORD '{{password}}' VALID UNTIL '{{expiration}}';" \
  default_ttl="1h" max_ttl="24h"
vault read database/creds/app   # short-lived creds, no restarts to rotate

# Transit: encryption without key-management pain
vault secrets enable transit
vault write -f transit/keys/orders
vault write transit/encrypt/orders plaintext=$(echo -n '4111...' | base64)

# Consul intention: the firewall rule for services
consul intention create -allow web api

notes.body: Build the secrets platform for a fictional microservices app: Vault with auto-unseal, KV + database + transit engines, OIDC for humans and Kubernetes auth for pods, deny-by-default least-privilege policies, Raft snapshots on schedule — and Consul with health-gated discovery plus a Connect mesh (intentions, mTLS, one gateway). I'm your instructor, and Module 14 is the associate tier around Kubernetes: KCNA for the vocabulary foundation, KCSA for the associate security lens, PCA for Prometheus observability, CCA for Cilium and eBPF networking, and CAPA for Argo GitOps — plus the consolidated associate-exam prep. notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
The associate-stack glossary — five exams, one vocabulary.
- **KCNA** — Kubernetes and cloud-native fundamentals: architecture, orchestration concepts, microservices, immutable infrastructure, declarative APIs, GitOps concepts, observability basics. The on-ramp: take it before CKA if Kubernetes is new.
- **KCSA** — cloud-native security associate: security overview, Kubernetes security fundamentals (RBAC, pod security, secrets, network policy), supply-chain basics. The prep ladder is KCSA → CKS.
- **PCA (Prometheus)** — metrics types: counter, gauge, histogram, summary. The PromQL trap: rate() over counters, never over gauges.
- **PromQL selectors and aggregation** — label selectors, rate(), and aggregation operators; alerting rules and the operator pattern.
- **service discovery (Prometheus)** — automatic target discovery for scraping.
- **CCA (Cilium)** — eBPF-powered networking: safe kernel programs replace kube-proxy iptables with eBPF maps.
- **Hubble** — Cilium's observability layer.
- **Cilium vs Calico policy depth** — Cilium enforces at L3–L7 (HTTP method/path-aware); Calico at L3/L4.
- **CAPA (Argo)** — GitOps with Argo: declared desired state in git, agents converge the cluster; git is the source of truth, the cluster is a cache.
- **Argo CD** — sync, drift detection, and automated sync policies; drift is detected, not debated.
- **Argo Rollouts** — progressive delivery (canary/blue-green) as Kubernetes CRDs with metric analysis.
- **sync waves/hooks** — ordering complex deploys: CRDs before the apps that need them.
- **associate exam format** — proctored online multiple-choice: vocabulary and concepts. The performance depth lives at CKA/CKAD/CKS.
- **recommended sequence** — KCNA → (PCA or CCA by interest) → CAPA → KCSA: breadth first, then the professional tier.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Build the breadth with light labs — vocabulary proven by doing, depth saved for the professional tier.
1. **KCNA vocabulary drill.** Diagram the Kubernetes architecture from memory (control plane vs nodes), then check against the docs; repeat until it's instant.
2. **PromQL.** Stand up Prometheus, scrape a test app, and run the canonical queries: `rate(http_requests_total[5m])`, aggregations by label, and one alerting rule. Deliberately run rate() over a gauge once — feel the trap, then never do it again.
3. **Cilium.** Install Cilium with kube-proxy replacement, apply an L7 network policy (HTTP method/path), and observe it in Hubble; compare with a Calico-style L3/L4 rule.
4. **Argo CD.** Point Argo CD at a git repo, watch drift detection flag a manual change, and let automated sync reconverge the cluster — git is truth, cluster is cache.
5. **Rollouts.** Define a canary Rollout with analysis steps; watch the progressive delivery proceed on metrics.
6. **KCSA map.** Walk the KCSA domain map against the CKS topics from Module 2; mark each CKS topic's associate-level prerequisite.
7. **Sequence.** Sit the ladder in order — KCNA → PCA/CCA → CAPA → KCSA — drilling the domain maps and vocabulary for each.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: web }
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate: { maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1 }
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: web } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: web } }
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: registry.example.com/web:1.4.2
        ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet: { path: /health, port: 8080 }
          periodSeconds: 5
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet: { path: /health, port: 8080 }
          periodSeconds: 15
        resources:
          requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }
          limits: { cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi }
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: web }
spec:
  selector: { app: web }
  ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 8080 }]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata: { name: web }
spec:
  rules:
  - host: web.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /, pathType: Prefix
        backend: { service: { name: web, port: { number: 80 } } }

blocks.body: Multi-stage: build fat → ship slim · COPY . . LAST · layers cache: slow-changing first
kubectl describe → logs → events → kubelet · requests schedule, limits kill · readiness gates traffic, liveness restarts
kubectl create/run/expose --dry-run=client -o yaml > f.yaml · aliases: k=kubectl · --force for recreates
init→validate→plan→apply · read the plan · state locked remotely · for_each over count · import then config
Multi-AZ everywhere · decouple with SQS · SG stateful / NACL stateless · Aurora=relational, DynamoDB=key-value · Savings Plans for baseline
PIM kills standing admin · Policy governs config, RBAC governs access · Zones > sets · Private Endpoints for PaaS · hub-spoke, non-transitive peering
SCPs bound, IAM grants · ABAC via tags · org Trail + Object Lock · KMS envelope encryption · WAF rate rules for floods
Git is truth, cluster is cache · Argo CD syncs · drift detected not debated · Rollouts for progressive delivery

answerBank.a: By job market target: AWS for startups/scale-ups breadth, Azure for enterprise/Microsoft shops. The concepts transfer ~80% (IAM/RBAC, VPC/VNet, S3/Blob). Pick one, go deep, then map the second in weeks not months.

CKA if you'll operate clusters; CKAD if you'll ship apps to them. Most learners benefit from CKA first — the admin mental model makes the developer exam easier. Both are performance-based: practice in live clusters.

Terraform for multi-cloud and marketability; CloudFormation/ARM for deep single-cloud shops. Learn Terraform first (the concepts transfer), then read the native tool. This module's Associate prep is Terraform.

answerBank.q: How do I practice CKS without a budget?
answerBank.a: Local clusters (kind/k3d) + Falco + a vulnerability scanner. The CKS skills (hardening, supply chain, runtime) all run locally. The exam environment is remote but the skills are identical.

answerBank.q: Zero trust — where do I actually start?
answerBank.a: Identity: phishing-resistant MFA everywhere + PIM for admins. That's 60% of the value. Then device posture, then microsegmentation. The module sequences SP 800-207 into this order.

Vault for multi-cloud/dynamic secrets/PKI-as-a-service; cloud-native secrets managers for single-cloud simplicity. Learn Vault's model (engines/auth/policies) — it teaches secrets thinking that transfers.
